title: A twin frozen on day one
allegory: The reference model is the trainee's twin, frozen on the day RL training began: it never writes a word, it only reads each word the trainee writes and says how likely it would have been to write it, and every word it would never have said costs the trainee a fine.
map: the twin, copied on day one and frozen in ice
π_ref: a copy of the pre-RLHF model, eval mode, no gradients
the twin reads each word the trainee writes

a twin who keeps learning alongside the trainee is never shocked
a reference aliased to (or refreshed from) the policy: KL reads 0, no anchor

cap.1: RL pushes a language model toward whatever the scorer loves. To stop it wandering too far, you first need a fixed spot to measure 'too far' from.
cap.2: The reward model is a proxy with errors, and RL is a search pointed straight at them. A KL penalty charges for drift, but drift is a distance, and a distance needs a starting point that stays put.
cap.3: D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref) only means something if π_ref is fixed. Gao, Schulman and Hilton indexed overoptimisation by KL from initialisation: proxy reward rises monotonically, gold reward peaks and falls along that axis.

cap.1: Before training starts, copy the model and freeze the copy. The trainee writes; the frozen twin only reads each word and says how likely it was to write it.
cap.2: The reference model is that frozen copy: the policy's own weights on day one, no gradients, eval mode. It never samples. It runs a forward pass on the policy's tokens to give ref_logits.
cap.3: π_ref is the pre-RLHF model held fixed. For each rollout it scores the generated tokens only, logits[:, -gen_len-1:-1], so the prefix the model did not choose is never charged.

cap.1: For every word the trainee might say next, compare two opinions: the trainee's and the twin's. Words the twin would almost never say cost the most.
cap.2: Per position: sum over the vocabulary of P·(log P − log Q), P from the policy, Q from the reference. Average over batch and position, multiply by kl_coef, subtract from the objective.
cap.3: Take log_softmax of both logits, then exp for P; never softmax then log. Direction D_KL(π‖π_ref) blows up where π_ref ≈ 0 but π is not, so gibberish is expensive and dropping old habits is cheap.

chapters.name: The moving twin

right.title: twin that moves with you
lines: the policy object itself, or a copy that trains
leash gone: reward up, text rots

chapters.verdict: A reference that can move is not a reference: copy it, freeze it, check it.

cap.1: If the twin learns alongside the trainee, it agrees with every word, so the drift reads zero forever. The leash is still there, tied to nothing.
cap.2: Hand the trainer the policy object itself instead of a copy and log π − log π_ref is 0 at every token. No error, no NaN: it looks exactly like running with kl_coef = 0.
cap.3: A broken penalty and a small one look identical on the reward curve. Audit it: reference in eval mode with no grad, generated-token slice only, P the policy and Q the reference. Then plot mean KL beside mean reward.

cap.1: The trainee writes, the scorer grades, and the frozen twin reads the very same words. Its opinions feed the fine that keeps the trainee from wandering off.
cap.2: Rollout: sample from the policy, score with the reward, run the reference on the same tokens. Since the twin never changes, its opinion of a given sample never changes: compute it once per batch.
cap.3: Cost: a second full copy of the weights in memory and a forward pass per batch, never a backward pass. In ARENA it is a separate frozen HookedTransformer beside the HookedTransformerWithValueHead.

chapters.name: Anchor, then steer
items: A frozen copy of the pre-RLHF model
It scores the trainee's words, never writes
Move it and the leash is gone
KL from it = how far training moved you

cap.1: The frozen twin measures how far training moved a model, and holds the rope that stops it moving too far. That is steering you can check.
cap.2: For any model fine-tuned with RL you can ask: how far from its reference is it now? KL from π_ref is that distance, and plotting it beside reward is how you catch reward hacking early.
cap.3: For understanding and steering AI, KL from the reference is the budget you spend to buy reward: the x-axis of Gao et al.'s gold-versus-proxy curves. GRPO keeps the same β·D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref) anchor.

coda.title: Frozen twin or moving twin: drift from day one (toy)

params.label: refresh the twin every N steps (300 = frozen)

readouts.label: what the leash is doing
readouts.f: N == 1 ? 'twin = trainee: KL reads 0, no leash at all' : (N >= 300 ? 'frozen: drift levels off where the pulls balance' : 'refreshed: each reset forgives the drift so far')

caption.1: Start frozen (N = 300) and watch the drift level off. Now drag N down: each refresh forgives the drift so far, and at N = 1 the leash does nothing at all.
caption.2: Toy: a steady reward pull against a KL leash tied to the twin. Frozen, the trainee settles where the pulls balance. Refreshed, every window adds more drift, so the total keeps growing.
caption.3: Locally KL is quadratic and reward linear, so a frozen π_ref gives equilibrium drift g/(2·kl_coef). Re-anchoring every step zeroes the penalty's gradient: plain reward ascent. Moving anchors bound steps, not journeys.

where_else: GRPO: the same β·D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref) term against a frozen reference
PPO and TRPO: a moving reference (last iteration's policy) that bounds each step, not the journey
Model diffing: compare a fine-tuned model with its base to see what training changed
Golden-file tests: compare each new output with a recording that is never silently updated

hamming.what: A frozen copy of the model from the moment RL fine-tuning began, used only to score the trainee's tokens so the KL penalty has a fixed point to measure drift from.
hamming.when: Whenever you fine-tune with RL against a learned or hand-written reward (RLHF, and GRPO's β·KL term), because any reward has errors that unchecked optimisation will find.
hamming.why: Without a fixed anchor there is no distance to penalise: a reference that moves with the policy reads zero drift forever, and the model walks off into text only the reward model loves.

object.title: The anchored bowl
object.subtitle: The objective as a bowl centred on the frozen twin and tipped by the reward. The bead is the model in training.

cap.1: The objective is a bowl centred on the frozen twin, tipped by the reward. The bead is the model in training: it rolls out a little, then the bowl holds it.
cap.2: Bowl = kl_coef × KL from the reference; tilt = the reward pulling one way. The bead settles where the two pulls balance, a short walk from day one.
cap.3: Near π_ref, KL is roughly quadratic in the parameter change (the Fisher metric) and reward roughly linear, so the optimum sits at the anchor plus the reward gradient shrunk by kl_coef.

cap.1: Pull the leash tight: steep walls, and the bead barely leaves the twin. Safe, but the model hardly improves.
cap.2: High kl_coef: the penalty dominates and the policy stays close to π_ref, so reward barely moves. That is the 'too high and it barely changes' failure.
cap.3: In this picture equilibrium drift scales as 1/kl_coef. ARENA defaults to kl_coef = 2.5, and its bonus adaptive controller retunes the coefficient to hold KL in a target band.

cap.1: Loosen the leash: the bowl flattens, the tilt wins, and the bead rolls far from the twin, toward text only the scorer loves.
cap.2: Low kl_coef: nothing holds the policy near the reference, so it follows the reward model into its errors. Mean reward keeps climbing while the samples get worse.
cap.3: The overoptimisation regime: as KL from initialisation grows, proxy reward keeps rising while gold reward peaks and falls (Gao, Schulman and Hilton, 2022).

cap.1: Now move the twin out to where the bead stopped. The bowl follows and the bead rolls on. Keep doing that and the leash never holds.
cap.2: Refreshing the reference re-centres the penalty on the current policy and forgives all drift so far. Aliasing it to the policy does this every step: KL always 0.
cap.3: A moving anchor bounds each step, not the journey: that is PPO's clip and TRPO's constraint against the last policy. RLHF's penalty works because π_ref never moves.

predict.q: You pass the policy object itself as the reference, with no copy. What does the KL penalty read?

options.t: 0 at every step, so the leash does nothing

predict.why: Both opinions come from the same weights, so log π − log π_ref is 0 everywhere. Nothing errors: it looks exactly like kl_coef = 0.

predict.q: What does the reference model do during a rollout?

options.t: Scores the trainee's own generated tokens
Writes its own answer to compare against
Scores the prompt tokens as well

predict.why: The penalty compares two opinions of the same words, so the reference runs one forward pass on the sampled sequence, sliced to the generated tokens: the model did not choose the prefix.

predict.q: PPO already clips every update. Why keep a frozen reference as well?

options.t: The clip limits each step; the reference limits the whole journey

predict.why: The clip compares with last iteration's policy, so it resets every batch. The frozen reference never moves, so drift adds up against it and the leash never resets.

object.where: Any fine-tune held to its starting point: GRPO's β·KL term, and golden-file tests that never auto-update the recording.
